Draft:

Every student should be required to join at least one extracurricular activity. Some students will resist this rule, arguing that school is for classes and that a forced activity wastes time they could spend on homework, a part-time job, or simply rest. I understand that concern, but I believe the principal's decision is a good one. Required participation gives students a place to belong, teaches skills that classrooms rarely reach, and often reveals talents that would otherwise stay hidden.

The most important benefit is belonging. Many students arrive at high school feeling invisible. They sit in large classes, eat lunch quickly, and go home without speaking to anyone outside their immediate circle. An activity changes that. Consider a student who joins the yearbook staff because it is the only elective left in his schedule. At first he only takes photographs of the cafeteria and the football field. Over the year he learns to interview classmates, meet deadlines, and argue with editors about page layouts. By spring he knows dozens of people across grade levels, and the adults who advised the staff have become mentors. Without the requirement, he might never have walked into that darkroom at all.

Activities also teach skills that tests do not measure. A student on the debate team learns to research both sides of an argument and to speak under pressure. A student on a soccer team learns that a missed pass affects everyone, and that practicing on a cold Tuesday matters more than any single game. Student council members learn budgeting when they must decide how to spend two thousand dollars from fundraising, and they learn compromise when three classes disagree about a homecoming theme. These lessons come from doing, and a requirement ensures that every student gets the chance to practice them.

Critics say that forcing participation turns activities into chores. This is true for some students who are assigned to a club they dislike. However, the requirement does not demand a specific choice. It demands only that students try something. A student who dislikes sports can choose chess, robotics, or the literary magazine. A student who dreads public speaking can join the photography club or the school garden. Most people discover what they enjoy only after trying several options, and the requirement guarantees that exploration happens. Many adults can point to a single hobby that changed the direction of their lives, and that hobby often began as something they only tried because they had to.

Finally, extracurricular activities connect learning to the wider world. Classrooms can explain how a government works, but the student council shows how a vote is counted and how a proposal becomes a policy. Classrooms can describe teamwork, but a band or a robotics team demands it every afternoon. These experiences prepare students for jobs, colleges, and civic life, where cooperation and initiative matter as much as grades.

Some will say that a single rule cannot fit every student. That is correct, which is why the rule should be broad enough to let each student find a fit. The principal's decision recognizes that school should do more than deliver information. It should help students become confident, connected, and curious people. For that reason, I agree that every student should participate in at least one extracurricular activity.
